doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Favorite records and what he would revisit in a time machine
summary: Monk Rowe asks about Kansas City and Green Onions. Dorn names doo wop, Ray Charles and Drifters records, and says he would like to witness Leiber and Stoller or Spector sessions.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution

blocks.x: I want to mention a couple of recordings to you and see if they have any significance: Wilbert Harrison’s recording of “Kansas City.”

“Kansas City.” Liked it, you know, not one of my — I mean it’s not a record that I go back to but remember, first of all, I was in junior high or maybe the first year of high school so it was a big record. And Mike and Jerry you know, wrote it, so I always had a sentimental thing about that.
There’s something about the groove on it that I think is pretty cool.
Yeah, oh no, no, no, it’s cool.
Like it. But once again, these are favorites of yours.
I like both of them but are they records I would put on? No. If they were on I wouldn’t take them off. But I wouldn’t put them on. You want to know a record I feel that way about?
Yeah, but I’m not — see again I’m not —

You want to hear a groove? You want to hear somebody sing? “Leave My Woman Alone” by Ray Charles. “I’m Moving On” by Ray Charles. Clyde McPhatter “The Treasure of Love” or “Without Love.” Any of those Drifters records. “Save the Last Dance,” “This Magic Moment,” The Coasters records that Mike and Jerry made, “Charlie Brown,” “Yakity Yak,” “Shopping for Clothes.” Certain Motown records — and I can name you 500 doo wop records that I love you know.
Well along the same lines, if you could get in a time machine and go be an assistant producer on some records that have been made over the years.

Mike and Jerry, or Spector. “Be My Baby” and “Da Do Run Run,” get out. Do you have any idea what it must have felt like in the room that night? But if I could be in a time machine the first thing I’d do is go back to when Jayne Mansfield was about 25. I think that would be a good thing to do in a time machine, and then go to the studio.

I mean there are so many records like that, you know I just mentioned a couple. But I mean how’d you like to be there? I’d just like to be there when they recorded “What’d I Say.” You think that would be a nice feeling?
